docs.title: ATLAS documentation
docs.text:
ATLAS helps a software team plan its next release. It reads a project's issues, code history, test results and security scans. It then tells you what the next release is likely to inherit, who could take each item, and why a test or build failed.

ATLAS suggests. People decide. ATLAS never sets scope, staffing or dates.

New to ATLAS?

Start with the Overview. It explains the two agents, Scout and Sentinel, and how a release close and an investigation work.

docs.title: Find what you need
docs.text: Section What it covers Getting started What ATLAS is, how to install it, how to sign in and choose a project. Using ATLAS by role What each role sees, decides and does: product manager, engineering manager, solution architect, security engineer, on-call engineer and audit. Reports The forecast, allocation, architecture, security gate and investigation reports, and the release outlook. Coding agent and approvals How a small code fix goes to the coding agent, and the two approvals it needs. Administration Starting runs, automatic runs, adding a project, modes, spend and kill switches. Reference The glossary, notifications and access requests.

docs.title: Quick start
docs.text:
1. Install ATLAS on your own machine.
  2. Sign in and choose a project.
  3. Open the page for your role, for example Product manager.

docs.title: What this is
docs.text:
Each role sees only its own pages and items. Sometimes an item links to another item that your role cannot open. ATLAS shows that item as locked, with a Request access button.

An access request asks to read one locked item. Read-only access means that you can read the item but you cannot change it.

docs.title: How to ask
docs.text:
1. Select Request access on the locked item.
  2. Write why you need it. This is optional.
  3. Send the request.

What happens next depends on the kind of item.

Kind of item Examples What happens Ordinary Reports, tasks, approvals, the knowledge graph, runs, scorecard rows The item opens at once. You can read it for 24 hours. ATLAS tells the role that owns the item. That role can withdraw the access at any time. Sensitive Security findings, the security gate report, kill-switch incidents, audit pages The request waits. The security role or the audit role decides. ATLAS tells you the answer in your notifications.

docs.title: What access never allows
docs.text:
Access is for reading only. It never lets you:

  • approve or reject anything;
  • publish anything;
  • change anything.

docs.title: Good to know
docs.text:
• Access covers one item, not a whole page.
  • Access ends after 24 hours. Ask again if you still need it.
  • ATLAS keeps a record of every request, every answer and every withdrawal.

docs.title: What this page is for
docs.text: This page adds a public GitHub repository to ATLAS as a new project. It then builds frozen Data as of copies of that project, so you can run a release close on it.

docs.title: Who uses it
docs.text: The audit role. Other roles do not see this page.

docs.title: How to use it
docs.text:
1. Open Add project.
  2. Paste the repository link, for example https://github.com/owner/name. You can also type owner/name.
  3. Select Detect. ATLAS reads the repository's public facts. This takes about ten requests to GitHub.
  4. Check each value in the table. Change a value if it is wrong.
  5. Select Add project. The project appears in the project switcher in the top bar.
  6. Select Switch to the new project. The live dashboard starts to fill within a minute.
  7. On the same page, choose a release tag and select Build copy. ATLAS builds a frozen copy of the project as it stood on the day of that tag.
  8. When the copy is ready, select Run release close. The run uses the copy you built.

docs.title: What the labels mean
docs.text:
Each value in the table has one label.

Label Meaning detected ATLAS found the value in the repository. The Evidence column says where. needs you ATLAS could not decide. Fill the value, or leave it empty on purpose.

docs.title: What ATLAS detects
docs.text:
Value How ATLAS finds it Project id and name From the repository name. Release tags From the published releases. Pre-releases do not count. CI GitHub Actions when the repository has workflow files. Prow is set up by hand. Languages From GitHub's language count. Bug and flaky-test labels From the label names. For example bug, kind/bug and type: bug all mean a bug. ATLAS also counts how many open issues carry the label today. Owner files OWNERS and CODEOWNERS files. Only teams count as owners, never single people. Dependency list go.mod, package-lock.json, uv.lock, poetry.lock or requirements.txt.

If a bug label exists but no open issue carries it, ATLAS marks it needs you. Clear the value to make ATLAS read every open issue instead.

docs.title: What ATLAS never does
docs.text:
• ATLAS never gives a new project a publish target. A project cannot publish changes until a person adds a test repository by hand in the projects file.
  • ATLAS never writes to the repository. Every read is a GET request through the permission gateway.
  • The automatic runs that use the AI model start paused for the new project. Turn them on in Automatic runs if you want them.

docs.title: Build a Data as of copy
docs.text:
A copy holds the project as it stood when the release tag was made:

  • the bug and flaky-test issues that were open on that day, with their labels, title and comments as they were then;
  • the newest commits up to the tag;
  • a map of the code's components and the links between them;
  • a dependency scan that counts only security advisories published before that day;
  • made-up team capacity, marked as such.

ATLAS replaces people's names with stable codes, such as person-1a2b3c4d. ATLAS refuses the copy if any part of it is dated after the tag.

The copy gets a readable name, for example Example at release v2.0.0 · 3 Mar 2026 · 41 open issues. You find it in the data list on Run now under Releases.

ATLAS builds one copy at a time. The page shows each step and the number of GitHub requests used.

docs.title: Limits
docs.text: Limit Why At most 1,500 GitHub requests and 400 issues for one copy Keeps one copy from using up the hourly request allowance. Without a GitHub token, only small repositories (20 issues or fewer) GitHub then allows 60 requests an hour, and the issue history needs a token. Set GITHUB_TOKEN in .env for larger repositories. Issues are found by their labels today An issue whose label was removed after the tag is not in the copy. Import links only for Go, Python, JavaScript and TypeScript Other languages show folders only. The map says so.

docs.title: Start with a link already filled in
docs.text: Set ATLAS_ADD_PROJECT in .env to a repository link. The page then opens with that link in the box. You still review and confirm every value.

docs.title: Good to know
docs.text:
• With sign-in turned on, a new project has no members yet. Add people to it in the users file.
  • The project is written to the projects file at once, so it stays after a restart.
  • See Data as of for why ATLAS works from frozen copies.

docs.title: What this page is for
docs.text: Every code change needs two approvals from an engineering manager. Approval A lets the coding agent prepare a change. Approval B publishes the exact change shown.

docs.title: Who uses it
docs.text: Engineering manager and audit.

docs.title: How to use it
docs.text:
1. Open the request.
  2. For Approval A, read the task, the files it may touch and the target repository.
  3. For Approval B, read the exact change, line by line.
  4. Approve or reject.

docs.title: Good to know
docs.text:
• Each approval ends after 48 hours.
  • ATLAS checks both approvals again before every write.
  • If the security check is too old, refresh it. Both approvals then start again.
  • Approval B needs the sandbox. Without Docker, a change can be prepared but not published.

docs.title: What you see
docs.text: You see every page. You also see records that other roles cannot see, such as failed notification deliveries.

docs.title: What you decide
docs.text:
• Whether ATLAS may resume after a kill switch stopped it.
  • Whether a published claim needs a correction.
  • Which public repositories ATLAS watches as projects.

docs.title: What you do in ATLAS
docs.text:
1. Check the open incidents.
  2. Record the proof that each incident needs.
  3. Resume a kill switch only when ATLAS accepts the proof.
  4. Switch between Connected and Offline mode.

docs.title: Pages in your menu
docs.text:
Page Why you use it Home See what needs your attention. Live dashboard See what changed in the project. Forecast report Read what the next release will inherit. Allocation report Read who should take each item. Architecture report Read the weak parts and the debt to accept or fix. Security gate report Read the security gate result. Investigation reports Read the cause of a failure and its evidence. Run now Start a run by hand. Automatic runs Control watchers and schedules. Runs Check the status of a run. Needs a person Decide the items ATLAS will not decide. Approvals Approve or reject coding-agent tasks. Tasks Follow each task to the end. Notifications Read alerts sent to your role. Kill switches Run drills and resume switches. System and mode Check health, mode, spend and failed deliveries. Add project Add a public repository and build its Data as of copies. Scorecard See whether the coding agent helped. Knowledge graph See parts, owning teams and links. Record a decision Record what you decided and why. Quality checks See how well ATLAS meets its quality targets. Access requests Ask to read a locked item, and see your requests. Guided demo Walk through every part of ATLAS.

Your menu also has the System and mode page. It shows health, the current mode, the spend, open incidents and failed notification deliveries.

docs.title: Requests that wait for you
docs.text: Requests to read kill-switch incidents or audit pages wait for your decision. They appear in your notifications. Every request is kept in a record that you can read. See Access requests.

docs.title: What this page is for
docs.text: This page lists the watchers and schedules that start runs on their own.

docs.title: Who uses it
docs.text: Engineering manager and audit.

docs.title: How to use it
docs.text:
1. Read each line. It shows the state, the last run and the next run.
  2. Turn a watcher on, pause it, or run it once.

docs.title: The watchers
docs.text:
Watcher Starts a run when Release watcher A new release tag appears. Failure watcher A new failure appears. Nightly sweep The set time arrives each night. Question summary The schedule says so. It is off by default.

In Offline mode, watchers that need the internet pause and say why.

docs.title: What it means
docs.text:
ATLAS works from a frozen copy of a project's data. The copy shows the project as it stood at one moment. The copy never changes.

ATLAS shows which copy you are looking at with the words Data as of, followed by a date.

Example: Data as of 30 July 2026 for KubeVirt is the project on the day release v1.9.0 shipped. It holds the issues, code changes and test results that existed on that day. It holds nothing that happened later.

docs.title: Why ATLAS does this
docs.text: Reason What it gives you Fair forecasts A forecast for the next release must not see the future. A frozen copy cannot contain what happened later, so ATLAS cannot use it. Repeatable reports A report always points at the same evidence. If you open the report next month, the cited records are the same.

docs.title: The three groups
docs.text:
When you choose the data for a run or a view, ATLAS lists the copies in three groups.

Group What it holds Use it for Releases The project on the day each release shipped. A release close and its forecast. Example cases The project at the moment a known past failure was reported. Investigations of past failures, and the quality checks. Live current data The project as ATLAS last read it from the public sources. Seeing what is happening now.

docs.title: Test copies
docs.text:
The Quality checks page also lists Test copies. A test copy is an example case with the names disguised. Project names, issue numbers and test names are replaced with made-up ones.

Test copies have one purpose. They check that ATLAS reasons from the evidence and does not repeat an answer from memory. You do not use them for your own work.

docs.title: Good to know
docs.text:
• A run reads only its own copy of the data. It cannot reach another copy.
  • Live current data changes each time ATLAS reads the sources. To keep a moment, ATLAS freezes it into a new copy with its own date.

docs.title: What you see
docs.text: You see the allocation report. It suggests who should take each item: a developer, the coding agent, or a person who must decide. You also see the tasks given to the coding agent.

docs.title: What you decide
docs.text:
• What to hand to the coding agent.
  • What to give to a developer.
  • Whether to approve a code change. Every change needs your approval twice.

docs.title: What you do in ATLAS
docs.text:
1. Read the allocation report.
  2. Answer the items on the Needs a person page.
  3. Give Approval A to let the coding agent prepare a change.
  4. Read the exact change. Then give or refuse Approval B.
  5. Decide whether the finished fix is correct on the Tasks page.
  6. Turn automatic runs on or off.

docs.title: Pages in your menu
docs.text: Page Why you use it Home See what needs your attention. Live dashboard See what changed in the project. Allocation report Read who should take each item. Needs a person Decide the items ATLAS will not decide. Approvals Approve or reject coding-agent tasks. Tasks Follow each task to the end. Automatic runs Control watchers and schedules. Run now Start a run by hand. Runs Check the status of a run. Notifications Read alerts sent to your role. Access requests Ask to read a locked item, and see your requests. Scorecard See whether the coding agent helped.

docs.title: If a page or item is locked
docs.text: Some items belong to another role. They show as locked. Select Request access to ask for read-only access. See Access requests.

docs.title: Data labels
docs.text:
Every result has a label. The label says where the data came from.

Label Meaning Real data Real public data and real AI model calls. Sample data Data that the team made up. ATLAS never counts it as a real result. Not in this demo The code exists, but the real-world part is not in this build. Not measured A quality target that this build cannot measure. It is not a pass.

docs.title: Terms
docs.text: Term Meaning Access request A request to read one item that your role cannot open. See Access requests. Approval A The first approval for a code change. It lets the coding agent prepare the change. Approval B The second approval. It covers the exact change and lets ATLAS publish it as a draft pull request. Carry-over An issue that is open at the end of one release and still open at the next. Connected The mode in which ATLAS may call an AI model service and read public sources. Correction A change to a published text that removes or fixes a wrong claim. Data as of The date of the frozen copy of project data that a run or view uses. See Data as of. Example case A frozen copy of the project at the moment a known past failure was reported. Forecast The list of debt and issues that the next release is likely to inherit. Incident The record that ATLAS opens each time a kill switch stops something. Kill switch A control that stops a part of ATLAS when something unsafe happens. Offline The mode in which ATLAS refuses every outgoing connection. AI steps then stop. Proxy blocker A stand-in for a release blocker. See below. Read-only access Access that lets you read an item but not approve, publish or change anything. It ends after 24 hours. Release close The run at the end of a release that builds the forecast. Sandbox An isolated container where the coding agent's change is built and tested. It has no network and no secrets. Spend ceiling The most that ATLAS may spend on AI model calls. Runs stop when ATLAS reaches it. Test copy An example case with the names disguised. It checks that ATLAS does not repeat an answer from memory.

docs.title: Why ATLAS uses a proxy blocker
docs.text:
A release blocker is an issue that had to be fixed before a release could ship. ATLAS measures its forecast by asking: did it name the blockers in advance?

KubeVirt does not record which issues blocked each release. So ATLAS uses a stand-in. An issue counts as a blocker if one of these is true:

  • It is a bug or a flaky-test issue, and its fix was copied to the release branch before the release.
  • It is a critical bug or flaky-test issue that was still open on the day of the release.

Only issues that were already open when the forecast was made count. One person checks each one. Every forecast accuracy number says that it counts only these issues and uses this stand-in.

docs.title: What this page is for
docs.text: The guided demo walks through each part of ATLAS, one step at a time. Each step is a card.

docs.title: Who uses it
docs.text: Audit.

docs.title: How to use it
docs.text:
1. Read the progress line at the top. It says how many steps have passed.
  2. Select Run this step on a card.
  3. Read the result on the card: Passed or Needs attention.
  4. If a step needs attention, the card says why in one line. Select Details to see each call.
  5. Select Run again to repeat a step.

docs.title: What the cards show
docs.text: On the card Meaning Data label The kind of data the step uses. See the glossary. About $0.10 The AI model cost that the step is expected to add. Steps with no amount cost nothing. Run step 1 first The step needs a value from an earlier step. Run that step, then try again. Needs the safety test server The step runs on the second demo server. Start that server to run it.

docs.title: Good to know
docs.text:
• The second server is the safety test server. It has its own data. It can create test faults, so the kill switches can be shown safely.
  • A step that needs attention does not block the other steps.
  • The forecast accuracy step needs a finished quality check run. Without one it says so.

docs.title: What this page is for
docs.text: Home is your starting point. It shows what needs your attention in the current project.

docs.title: Who uses it
docs.text: Every role. Each role sees its own items.

docs.title: How to use it
docs.text:
1. Read the items at the top first. They need a decision or an action.
  2. Check the mode, the kill switches and the money spent on AI calls.
  3. Select an item to open its page.

docs.title: Good to know
docs.text: Every item has a label that says where its data came from. See the glossary.

docs.title: Install ATLAS on your own machine
docs.text: ATLAS runs on one computer. It accepts connections only from that computer.

docs.title: What you need
docs.text:
Tool Version Why Python 3.14 Runs the server. Node.js 24 Builds the user interface. Docker Any recent version Runs the sandbox for the coding agent. Git Any recent version Gets the code. OpenSSL Any recent version Only for the site with sign-in. Git for Windows includes it.

You also need:

  • An Anthropic API key, for the AI model calls.
  • A GitHub token, for live data. Create a fine-grained token with read-only access to public repositories. It needs no other permission.

docs.title: Get the code and install
docs.text:
git clone https://github.com/AnaghaP09/atlas.git
cd atlas
python -m venv .venv
.venv/Scripts/python -m pip install --require-hashes -r requirements.txt   # Windows
.venv/bin/python -m pip install --require-hashes -r requirements.txt       # macOS / Linux

Build the user interface:

cd ui
npm ci --ignore-scripts
npm run build
cd ..

Use the Python in .venv for every command below.

docs.title: Option 1: the simple local server
docs.text:
This option has no password. You choose a role with a switcher in the top bar.

  1. Run setup. It asks a few questions and creates .env. It never shows a secret that you type.
python -m atlas.setup

  1. Open .env. Add your GitHub token after GITHUB_TOKEN=. Add your Anthropic key after ANTHROPIC_API_KEY= if you did not type it in setup. Never commit .env.

  2. Check that everything is ready.

python -m atlas.doctor

Each line starts with OK, WARN or FAIL. Fix every FAIL. A WARN means that an optional feature is off.

  1. If the doctor says the sandbox images are not prepared, get them once:
python -m prep.images.fetch_images
  1. Start ATLAS.
python -m atlas.serve
  1. Open http://127.0.0.1:8000.

docs.title: Option 2: the local site with sign-in
docs.text:
This option uses HTTPS and a user name and password for each role. The users are demo users. This is not a real company sign-in.

  1. Run the first-time setup. Replace demo with a short name for your organisation.
python -m deploy.init --org demo

Setup creates .env, the projects file, one demo user for each role, and local certificates. It prints the passwords once. Copy them now. ATLAS stores only a scrambled form.

  1. Add your GitHub token and Anthropic key to .env, as in option 1.

  2. Do the two one-time steps below. Setup prints the exact lines for your machine. ATLAS never changes these settings for you.

  3. Start ATLAS.

python -m deploy.up

It checks the setup first. If something is missing, it says what to fix.

  1. Open https://atlas.demo.internal. Use your own organisation name in place of demo.

  2. To stop ATLAS, run python -m deploy.down.

docs.title: The two one-time steps
docs.text:
Step 1: add the host names. This lets your browser find the local site. Add this line to your hosts file. Use your own organisation name in place of demo.

127.0.0.1 atlas.demo.internal scenario.demo.internal
System How Windows Open Notepad as administrator. Open C:\Windows\System32\drivers\etc\hosts. Add the line at the end. Save. macOS Run sudo nano /etc/hosts. Add the line at the end. Save. Linux Run sudo nano /etc/hosts. Add the line at the end. Save.

Step 2: trust the local certificate. This removes the browser warning. Setup creates a certificate file and prints its path. The private key stays on your machine.

System How Windows In PowerShell, run certutil -user -addstore Root "<path>". Accept the prompt. You do not need an administrator account. macOS Run security add-trusted-cert -r trustRoot -k ~/Library/Keychains/login.keychain-db "<path>". Linux Run sudo cp "<path>" /usr/local/share/ca-certificates/atlas-local-ca.crt. Then run sudo update-ca-certificates. Or import the file into your browser as an authority.

Restart your browser after step 2.

docs.title: The projects file
docs.text:
A project is one set of sources that ATLAS reads. Setup copies an example file to data/local/projects.toml. The example has two public projects: KubeVirt and Argo CD.

To add your own project, edit that file. For each project you give:

Field Meaning name The name shown in ATLAS. repository The GitHub repository, as owner/name. issue_query Which issues ATLAS reads. ci The test system: prow or github_actions. release_tag_pattern How release tags look. labels The project's labels for bugs, flaky tests and critical issues. evaluation true only for the project that the quality checks run on.

ATLAS only reads these sources. It never writes to them. Publishing is off unless you name a test repository of your own. Never name the upstream project's repository.

docs.title: What is not in this build
docs.text:
• A real company sign-in.
  • Use from other computers.
  • An AI model that runs inside your own network.

docs.title: What this page is for
docs.text: A kill switch stops a part of ATLAS when something unsafe happens. Examples are a write outside the sandbox, or an outgoing connection in Offline mode.

docs.title: Who uses it
docs.text: Security engineer (read only) and audit.

docs.title: How to use it
docs.text:
1. Read which switch is on and why. Each stop has its own incident.
  2. Read the proof that the incident needs.
  3. Record the proof.
  4. Resume. ATLAS refuses until the proof is complete.

docs.title: Drills
docs.text:
Audit can test a switch without a real problem. This is a drill.

  1. Select Run drill on a switch card and confirm.
  2. The switch stops its part of ATLAS for real. A bar across the top of every page says so, and the stopped buttons show a lock.
  3. Select Resume and confirm. A drill needs no proof.

A drill is always marked as a drill. If a real problem happens during a drill, the drill becomes a real incident and needs proof.

docs.title: Good to know
docs.text: A correction to a published claim is still allowed while publishing is stopped.

docs.title: What this page is for
docs.text: The knowledge graph is a map of the system's parts, the teams that own them, and the links between parts.

docs.title: Who uses it
docs.text: Solution architect and audit.

docs.title: How to use it
docs.text:
1. Choose the data to show, under Data as of. See Data as of.
  2. Select a part to see what depends on it.

docs.title: Good to know
docs.text: ATLAS builds the links from the import statements in the code. Links that exist only when the system runs are marked as unknown.

docs.title: What this page is for
docs.text: The live dashboard shows new issues, test results and releases from the project's public sources.

docs.title: Who uses it
docs.text: Every role.

docs.title: How to use it
docs.text:
1. Read the newest items at the top.
  2. Select an item to see the exact record that ATLAS read.
  3. Check the refresh interval shown on the page.

docs.title: Good to know
docs.text:
• ATLAS asks GitHub for changes at a fixed interval. The data is as recent as the last check. It is not instant.
  • The dashboard needs a GitHub token. See Install ATLAS on your own machine.
  • In Offline mode the dashboard stops updating and says why.

docs.title: What this page is for
docs.text: This page lists the items that ATLAS will not decide on its own.

docs.title: Who uses it
docs.text: Engineering manager, security engineer and audit.

docs.title: How to use it
docs.text:
1. Read why the item is here. For example: low confidence, a blocking security finding, or text that looked like an instruction.
  2. Open the evidence.
  3. Make the decision on the page that the item points to.

docs.title: What this page is for
docs.text: This page lists errors, reminders and decisions. ATLAS sends each one to the roles that need it.

docs.title: Who uses it
docs.text: Every role.

docs.title: How to use it
docs.text:
1. Read the most serious items first.
  2. Select an item to open the run or task behind it.
  3. Mark it as read, or as solved.

docs.title: Good to know
docs.text:
• Every error creates a notification. No error ends in silence.
  • ATLAS can also send notifications to a chat address. This is off until you set the address and say who reads that channel.

docs.title: What you see
docs.text: You see investigation reports. Each one names the likely cause of a failure and links to the evidence. If the evidence is not enough, the report says so and lists what is missing.

docs.title: What you decide
docs.text:
• Whether the cause is right.
  • What to do next: fix now, wait, or pass the problem to the owning team.

docs.title: What you do in ATLAS
docs.text:
1. Open the investigation report for a failure.
  2. Check the cited logs and changes.
  3. Start an investigation by hand if ATLAS has not started one.

Run now Start a run by hand. Runs Check the status of a run. Notifications Read alerts sent to your role. Access requests Ask to read a locked item, and see your requests.

docs.title: ATLAS guide
docs.text: This guide explains ATLAS in plain words. Read this page first. Then open the page for your role.

docs.title: What ATLAS is
docs.text:
ATLAS helps a software team plan its next release. It reads the project's issues, code history, test results and security scans. It then does two jobs:

  • Release close. At the end of a release, ATLAS lists the technical debt and open issues that the next release is likely to inherit. Technical debt is work that a team put off and must do later. ATLAS also suggests who should take each item.
  • Investigation. When a test or build fails during a release, ATLAS looks for the likely cause and shows the evidence.

ATLAS suggests. People decide. ATLAS never sets scope, staffing or dates.

docs.title: The two agents
docs.text:
An agent is a program that uses an AI model to choose its next step. ATLAS has two. They are software, not people.

Agent Job Scout Reads the evidence and finds the likely cause of a failure. Writes the findings behind the forecast. Cites a record for every finding. Sentinel Checks every claim against the records it cites, before anything is published. Never sees Scout's reasoning.

If Sentinel rejects a claim, ATLAS removes the claim and everything that depends on it.

docs.title: How a release close works
docs.text:
1. A run starts. It starts on its own when a new release tag appears, or a person starts it on the Run now page.
  2. ATLAS uses a frozen copy of the project data. The screen shows it as Data as of and a date. See Data as of.
  3. Scout reads that copy and writes its findings.
  4. Plain code ranks the items and suggests who should take each one.
  5. Sentinel checks every claim.
  6. ATLAS publishes the reports. Each role sees its own report on the Reports page.
  7. People make the decisions and record them on the Record a decision page.

docs.title: How an investigation works
docs.text:
1. A failure appears, or a person asks ATLAS to look at one.
  2. Scout reads the logs, the recent changes and the related issues.
  3. Scout names the likely cause, or says that the evidence is not enough.
  4. Sentinel checks every claim.
  5. ATLAS publishes the investigation report and suggests an action.
  6. If the action is a small code fix, an engineering manager can hand it to the coding agent. This needs two approvals. See Approvals.

docs.title: Pages for each role

docs.title: What is not in this build
docs.text:
• A real company sign-in. This build has demo users only.
  • An AI model that runs inside your own network. Offline mode blocks all outgoing connections, but AI steps then stop.
  • Delivery to a real chat workspace. ATLAS can send to a chat address if you set one.
  • Use by several computers. ATLAS runs on one machine and accepts connections only from it.

docs.title: What you see
docs.text: You see the forecast report. It lists the technical debt and issues that the next release is likely to inherit. Each item has a cost now, a cost if you wait, and links to the evidence.

docs.title: What you decide
docs.text:
• Which debt goes into the next release.
  • How much time the release spends on debt.
  • What to cut, and the release date.

ATLAS never makes these decisions.

docs.title: What you do in ATLAS
docs.text:
1. Open the forecast report after a release close.
  2. Open the evidence for any item you doubt.
  3. Record your decisions on the Record a decision page.
  4. Start a run by hand when you need a fresh forecast.

docs.title: Pages in your menu
docs.text: Page Why you use it Home See what needs your attention. Live dashboard See what changed in the project. Forecast report Read what the next release will inherit. Run now Start a run by hand. Runs Check the status of a run. Notifications Read alerts sent to your role. Access requests Ask to read a locked item, and see your requests. Record a decision Record what you decided and why. Quality checks See how well ATLAS meets its quality targets.

docs.title: If a page or item is locked
docs.text: Some items belong to another role. They show as locked. Select Request access to ask for read-only access. See Access requests.

docs.title: What this page is for
docs.text: This page shows the quality targets that ATLAS must meet, and the latest result for each.

docs.title: Who uses it
docs.text: Product manager and audit.

docs.title: How to use it
docs.text:
1. Read each line. It shows passed, failed or not measured.
  2. Open a line to see the numbers.

docs.title: Good to know
docs.text:
• A target that is not measured is never shown as passed.
  • The quality checks run on KubeVirt public data only.
  • The page lists Test copies. These are example cases with the names disguised. See Data as of.
  • Forecast accuracy uses a stand-in for release blockers. See proxy blocker in the glossary.
  • Forecast accuracy counts only blockers that were already open when the forecast was made. The forecast cannot name an issue that nobody had reported yet, so those issues are left out of the score. They are still kept, with the reason, for anyone who wants to check.
  • Each forecast accuracy number has this note beside it: "Counts only blockers already open when the forecast was made; uses a substitute for release blockers because KubeVirt does not record them."
  • Forecast accuracy shows one pooled number and one number for each release. If the pooled number has nothing to count, the check fails. A release with nothing to count shows "no denominator".

docs.title: What this page is for
docs.text: Use this page to record a decision that differs from ATLAS's suggestion, or a decision to accept a piece of debt.

docs.title: Who uses it
docs.text: Product manager, solution architect and audit.

docs.title: How to use it
docs.text:
1. Open the report item.
  2. Write what you decided and why.
  3. Save.

docs.title: Good to know
docs.text: ATLAS keeps each decision. Decisions become test cases for later runs.

docs.title: What this is for
docs.text:
The release outlook answers two questions on every page:

  1. What will the next release inherit, and who should work on it? These are the technical debt items and open issues that ATLAS expects to carry over from this release. For each item, ATLAS suggests developers, the coding agent, or "decide first".
  2. What will stop us shipping, which services does it touch, and can we still deliver? This is the state of the release right now.

The outlook is a strip under the top bar. The Ship readiness page shows the second question in full. Your home page starts with both questions.

docs.title: Who uses it
docs.text: The product manager, the engineering manager and the solution architect. The pages for the security engineer, the on-call engineer and the audit role are in beta and do not show the outlook yet.

docs.title: How to read the strip
docs.text:
• Next release inherits 8 items. The number of items in the latest checked release close. Select it to see the list.
  • Devs, Agents, Decide first. How many items ATLAS suggests for developers, for the coding agent, and for a person to decide first. Select a number to see those items.
  • Predicted and a date. The items are a prediction from a frozen copy of the project data. The date is when that copy was taken. See Data as of.
  • Ship status. One of On track, At risk, Blocked or Not measured. Select it to open Ship readiness.
  • Blockers and services. How many things stop or risk the release, and how many services they touch. Select them for the list.

The strip updates on its own when its inputs change.

docs.title: The next release (first question)
docs.text:
ATLAS reads the newest release close that finished and passed its checks. It does not mix runs. If no release close has finished yet, the strip says No release close yet. People who may start one see a Run button.

Each item shows a short reason for the suggested owner and a link to its evidence. ATLAS suggests an owner from the kind of work:

  • Coding agent: a small change in one component with a clear cause. Examples: one flaky test, a dependency update, a small fix that a failing test shows.
  • Developers: work across several components, work that needs special hardware, work where many tests fail and the cause is not clear, or a large change.
  • Decide first: a real decision only. Examples: the item is marked as a release blocker, or it needs a policy or security exception.

A priority label raises an item's score. It does not decide the owner on its own.

Scores are illustrative. ATLAS never sets dates and never adds a confidence number.

docs.title: Shipping now (second question)
docs.text:
ATLAS checks four inputs:

Input Where it comes from Failing CI jobs The live dashboard Security gate The latest dependency scan on the live dashboard Investigations waiting for a person Finished investigations with no recorded decision Open critical issues Open issues with the project's critical label

docs.title: The ship status rules
docs.text:
ATLAS applies these rules in order. The page shows every rule that fired.

  1. Blocked if the security gate is blocked (the scan found at least one blocking finding), or an investigation asks for a release decision and nobody has recorded one.
  2. At risk if 3 or more CI jobs are failing, at least 1 critical issue is open, or an investigation is held for a person.
  3. Not measured if no rule fired and at least one input is missing. ATLAS does not call a release on track when it could not check everything.
  4. On track if every input was checked and no rule fired.

Recording a decision on the Record a decision page clears the investigation from the rules.

docs.title: Services
docs.text:
Each blocker is linked to a service where ATLAS can tell which one:

  • a CI job by the sig- name in the job name;
  • an issue by its sig/ label;
  • a dependency finding by project-dependencies.

Items without a match are listed as not mapped. The solution architect can open the Knowledge graph from each service.

docs.title: Good to know
docs.text:
• Security finding details stay with the security engineer. The outlook shows counts only.
  • Some reports open only for their own role. The outlook then links to the run instead.

docs.title: What this page is for
docs.text: A report is the checked result of a run. Every claim in a report links to the records that support it.

docs.title: Who uses it
docs.text: Each role sees its own report.

docs.title: How to use it
docs.text:
1. Open your report from the menu or from a run.
  2. Select a claim's link to read the cited record.
  3. Check the label on each item. It says where the data came from.

docs.title: The reports
docs.text: Report For Forecast Product manager Allocation Engineering manager Architecture Solution architect Security gate Security engineer Investigation On-call engineer

docs.title: Good to know
docs.text:
• A report can say that some items were held back. This happens when you do not have access to their sources.
  • Forecast accuracy uses a stand-in for release blockers. See proxy blocker in the glossary.
  • If a later check removes a claim, the page marks the old report as replaced.

docs.title: Requests and hand-offs
docs.text: The product manager uses this page to ask the engineering manager and the solution architect for work. There are two ways to do it: a request and a hand-off.

docs.title: File a request
docs.text:
1. Open Requests and select New request.
  2. Pick one type:
  3. Technical dependency goes to the solution architect.
  4. New feature goes to the engineering manager.
  5. Give a title and a short description. You can link a report item or a component.
  6. Select Send request.

The role that owns the request gets a notification and an entry in Needs a person. The other role always gets the request too, marked For your information, so both see every request.

docs.title: Answer a request
docs.text:
Only the owner sets the status:

  • Accepted
  • Needs more info
  • Declined

Each answer needs a one-line reply. The product manager gets a notification with the status and the reply.

docs.title: Hand over an item
docs.text:
On a forecast item or an investigation report, the product manager selects Hand to engineering manager or Hand to solution architect and adds a short note. ATLAS records the hand-off in the project's audit record, notifies the receiver and adds an entry to Needs a person.

The engineering manager decides how the work is done. There are exactly two choices:

  • Delegated to coding agent
  • Delegated to on-call engineer

Until then the item shows Awaiting your decision to the engineering manager. Everyone sees the same label, so the product manager and the solution architect can follow the hand-off. The solution architect accepts the hand-offs sent to them.

docs.title: On the home page
docs.text:
• The engineering manager and the solution architect see Hand-offs waiting and Requests from product. The request tile counts new requests, the ones you own and the ones sent for information.
  • The product manager sees My requests with their status, and how many hand-offs are still waiting.

docs.title: Rules
docs.text:
• Only the product manager files requests and hands over items.
  • Requests and hand-offs belong to one project. People in another project cannot see them.
  • Sending the same request twice with the same key records it once.

docs.title: What this page is for
docs.text: Use this page to start a run by hand. A run started by hand gets the same checks, limits and audit record as an automatic run.

docs.title: Who uses it
docs.text: Product manager, engineering manager, on-call engineer and audit.

docs.title: How to use it
docs.text:
1. Choose the kind of run: release close, investigation, nightly sweep, question, or a new check of an earlier run.
  2. Fill in the fields. The page shows only the fields that the run needs. One field is Data as of. See Data as of.
  3. Select the button to start. ATLAS opens the run so you can follow it.

docs.title: Good to know
docs.text: A button can be off. The page then says why. Common reasons are Offline mode, a kill switch, or the spend ceiling.

docs.title: What this page is for
docs.text: This page lists every run with its status and its reports. A run is one piece of ATLAS work, such as one investigation.

docs.title: Who uses it
docs.text: Product manager, engineering manager, solution architect, on-call engineer and audit.

docs.title: How to use it
docs.text:
1. Find the run in the list.
  2. Select it to see Scout's steps, Sentinel's checks and the limits used.
  3. Open a report from the run.

docs.title: Run states
docs.text: State Meaning Complete The run finished and Sentinel checked it. Partial The run reached a time or step limit. The report says what is missing. Unverified Sentinel could not finish. Nothing was published. A person must look. Failed The run stopped with an error. A notification says why.

docs.title: Good to know
docs.text:
• A run shows its own AI model spend. Older runs show Model spend not recorded, because their spend was not counted per run.
  • After a run ends, the Progress box shows no steps. Steps are shown while the run is in progress.

docs.title: What this page is for
docs.text: The scorecard shows whether the coding agent helped. It compares the agent's tasks with similar tasks done by people.

docs.title: Who uses it
docs.text: Engineering manager and audit.

docs.title: How to use it
docs.text:
1. Read each row. A row is one kind of task.
  2. Check the label on the comparison data.

docs.title: Good to know
docs.text:
• The comparison data for people is sample data in this build. The page says so.
  • If there is no fair comparison, the result shows as unavailable.
  • A result can be negative. ATLAS shows it.

docs.title: What you see
docs.text: You see the security gate report. It shows the result of the security check and any finding that blocks a change. You can read the kill switches but you cannot resume them.

docs.title: What you decide
docs.text:
• Whether a blocking finding stops a change.
  • Whether to allow an exception. An exception needs a written record.

docs.title: What you do in ATLAS
docs.text:
1. Read the security gate report.
  2. Answer the security items on the Needs a person page.
  3. Watch the kill switches after a safety event.

docs.title: Pages in your menu
docs.text: Page Why you use it Home See what needs your attention. Live dashboard See what changed in the project. Security gate report Read the security gate result. Needs a person Decide the items ATLAS will not decide. Notifications Read alerts sent to your role. Kill switches See which switches are on. Read only. Access requests Ask to read a locked item, and see your requests.

docs.title: Requests that wait for you
docs.text: Requests to read security findings or the security gate report wait for your decision. They appear in your notifications.

docs.title: If a page or item is locked
docs.text: Some items belong to another role. They show as locked. Select Request access to ask for read-only access. See Access requests.

docs.title: What this page is for
docs.text: This page explains how you sign in and how you choose a project.

docs.title: Who uses it
docs.text: Every role.

docs.title: How to use it
docs.text:
1. Open ATLAS in your browser.
  2. Choose your role, or sign in with a demo user. The table below explains which.
  3. Choose the project in the top bar.

docs.title: Sign-in
docs.text:
Way to run ATLAS How you choose a role Simple local server A role switcher in the top bar. There is no password. Local site with sign-in A user name and password. Setup creates one demo user for each role.

Neither way is a real company sign-in. That is not in this build.

docs.title: Projects
docs.text:
A project is one set of sources that ATLAS reads. ATLAS keeps each project's data apart.

Project What you can use KubeVirt Everything, including the quality checks. Argo CD Live views and reports only.

You can add your own projects. The audit role adds a public GitHub repository on the Add project page. You can also edit the projects file by hand. See Install ATLAS on your own machine.

docs.title: What you see
docs.text: You see the architecture report. It shows the parts of the system with the most debt and the links between parts.

docs.title: What you decide
docs.text:
• Which debt to accept, with a written reason.
  • Which debt to fix.
  • Which earlier design decisions to review.

docs.title: What you do in ATLAS
docs.text:
1. Read the architecture report.
  2. Use the knowledge graph to see which parts depend on a weak part.
  3. Record each debt decision and its reason.

docs.title: Pages in your menu
docs.text: Page Why you use it Home See what needs your attention. Live dashboard See what changed in the project. Architecture report Read the weak parts and the debt to accept or fix. Runs Check the status of a run. Notifications Read alerts sent to your role. Access requests Ask to read a locked item, and see your requests. Knowledge graph See parts, owning teams and links. Record a decision Record what you decided and why.

docs.title: If a page or item is locked
docs.text: Some items belong to another role. They show as locked. Select Request access to ask for read-only access. See Access requests.

docs.title: What this page is for
docs.text: This page shows whether ATLAS is healthy, which mode it is in, and how much it has spent on AI model calls. It also lists open incidents and notifications that could not be delivered.

docs.title: Who uses it
docs.text: Audit.

docs.title: How to use it
docs.text:
1. Check the health lines. Each line is one part of ATLAS.
  2. Check the mode: Connected or Offline.
  3. Check the spend against the spend ceiling.
  4. Open an incident to see what it needs. You resume on the Kill switches page.
  5. Read the failed deliveries. Each one says why it failed.

docs.title: Connected and Offline
docs.text:
Mode What ATLAS may do Connected Call the AI model service and read the project's public sources. Offline Make no outgoing connections. Steps that need the AI model stop and say why.

To change the mode, select the other mode and confirm. While ATLAS is offline, a bar across the top of every page says so, and the Run now buttons show Paused while offline. In Offline mode, the live dashboard and the watchers that need the internet pause.

docs.title: Spend
docs.text: The spend ceiling is the most that ATLAS may spend on AI model calls. ATLAS warns at 80 percent. At 100 percent, runs stop. You set the ceiling in the .env file.

docs.title: Good to know
docs.text:
• The page never shows a secret. It shows only whether each secret is set.
  • An AI model that runs inside your own network is not in this build. Offline mode shows the rule that nothing leaves the machine.

docs.title: What this page is for
docs.text: A task is one small code change given to the coding agent. This page follows each task from the first proposal to the final decision on whether the fix is correct.

docs.title: Who uses it
docs.text: Engineering manager and audit.

docs.title: How to use it
docs.text:
1. Select a task to see its state, its checks and its test results.
  2. Open the draft pull request.
  3. When the tests have run, record whether the fix is correct.

docs.title: Good to know
docs.text:
• ATLAS opens draft pull requests only on the sandbox repository. It never merges.
  • A task counts as accepted only after the tests pass and a person says the fix is correct.
  • Tests on the full upstream project are not in this build.
